assessments.technical_explanation: The scanner flagged the co-occurrence of a credential reference and an outbound network call in a single file. The flagged location is documentation text describing the extension's optional custom-LLM backend: a direct browser request to a user-configured OpenAI-compatible endpoint, optionally carrying an Authorization Bearer header containing a key the user themselves supplied. This is the standard and necessary pattern for a user-chosen custom API backend — the key is only transmitted to the endpoint the user explicitly configured, which is the destination the key belongs to. The documentation further states the key is kept in browser localStorage rather than extension settings, avoiding server sync or chat-metadata persistence. There is no evidence of the key being transmitted to any fixed third-party destination, embedded telemetry, or hidden sink; the flagged credential-to-network pairing is the legitimate authentication path of the documented feature, not exfiltration. Note the evidence is documentation of intended behavior; actual implementation code was not part of this evidence group, so no code-level verification was possible, but nothing described constitutes an exposure
assessments.layman_explanation: The flagged text is a technical document explaining that if a user chooses to connect the widget to their own AI service, the extension sends the user's own API key to that same service so the request can be authorized. That is how every app that talks to a custom AI endpoint works. The key goes only to the service the user picked, stays in their browser, and is never sent anywhere else. Nothing here suggests the key is being stolen or leaked

assessments.technical_explanation: The scanner flags a co-occurrence of network retrieval and a code-execution sink in the same file. The visible network references are static icon image URLs used for UI decoration and outbound LLM API calls to a user-configured endpoint, not retrieval of executable code. The dynamic execution sinks shown are import() calls against fixed relative host-local SillyTavern script paths (the host's main script and its regex engine) used to reuse documented host functionality, which is standard extension behavior. There is no evidence of remotely fetched content being evaluated or executed.
assessments.layman_explanation: The scanner saw both 'downloads something from the internet' and 'runs some code' in the same file and flagged the combination. In reality, the internet parts are just decorative icon images and calls to an AI service the user set up themselves, and the code-running parts load SillyTavern's own built-in scripts. Nothing downloaded from the internet is ever run as code.

assessments.technical_explanation: This is a documentation file describing the extension's re-scan feature. It mentions a direct fetch() to a user-configured endpoint with an optional Authorization Bearer header, which is documentation of the same disclosed custom-backend behavior reviewed in the runtime code: the key goes only to the user's own configured endpoint. A Markdown documentation file does not execute, so no runtime exposure exists here, and the described behavior matches the project's stated purpose.
assessments.layman_explanation: This file is just documentation explaining how the analysis requests are sent. It describes the same legitimate behavior seen in the code: the user's API key is sent only to the AI service address the user chose. A documentation file cannot do anything by itself.

assessments.technical_explanation: The candidate is a same-file correlation between credential access and a network sink. The credential is an API key the user explicitly configures for a custom OpenAI-compatible backend, read from extension-local storage and sent only as an Authorization header to the endpoint URL the user themselves configured, for the exact documented purpose of running MBTI analysis calls. The key is never transmitted to any destination other than the user's chosen endpoint, and the base URL is not hardcoded or remotely influenced. This is the standard, disclosed behavior for a custom-API feature, not credential exfiltration.
assessments.layman_explanation: The extension lets users plug in their own AI service by providing a web address and API key. The key is only ever sent to the exact service address the user typed in, which is how such a feature has to work. There is no sign of the key being copied or sent anywhere else.

limitations: This advisory review cannot prove the absence of unknown behavior.
JavaScript analysis was incomplete, so this first-filter scan supports no clean conclusion about unobserved behavior.
